derivations.claim: If $n=0$, the codomain and image are both the zero group, so the cokernel is trivial and has order $1=|\det A|$. Now suppose $n>0$. Multiplication on the left or right by an integer matrix with determinant $\pm1$ preserves the isomorphism type of the cokernel and preserves the absolute determinant: left multiplication changes the basis of the target, and right multiplication changes the basis of the domain.

Among all matrices obtained from $A$ by such row and column operations, choose one whose least nonzero absolute entry is as small as possible; by swaps and a sign change, place that positive entry $d$ in position $(1,1)$. If any entry in its first row or column is not divisible by $d$, Euclidean division and a row or column subtraction produce a nonzero remainder strictly between $0$ and $d$, which contradicts the minimality of $d$. Clear the first row and column by subtracting multiples of the first column and row. If an entry $b$ in the remaining submatrix were not divisible by $d$, add its row to the first row, write $b=kd+r$ with $0<r<d$, and subtract $k$ times the first column from its column; swapping that column with the first would again give a smaller nonzero pivot. Hence $d$ divides the remaining submatrix.

Apply the same finite pivot procedure to the remaining submatrix. Induction gives a diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0,\ldots,0)$ with each $d_i>0$, obtained by unimodular row and column operations. Its cokernel is $\bigoplus_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/d_i\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z^{n-r}$. Thus it is finite exactly when $r=n$, equivalently when $\det A\ne0$; then its order is $\prod_i d_i=|\det A|$. The operations in step 1.1 preserve both conclusions for the original matrix. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link (a finite disjoint union of oriented smoothly embedded circles,
[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]) with $r\ge1$ components,
and let $X_L:=S^3\setminus L$. Then $X_L$ is a connected smooth $3$-manifold
without boundary, and in particular is path-connected, locally path-connected
and semilocally simply connected; moreover $X_L$ has the homotopy type of a
finite CW complex
([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]). Consequently the
covering-space classification
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]) applies to $X_L$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Radial motion in each punctured normal disk gives a deformation retraction from $S^3\setminus J$ to $X$. By [F1], Alexander duality identifies $H_1(S^3\setminus J;\mathbb Z)$ with $\widetilde H^1(J;\mathbb Z)=\bigoplus_iH^1(J_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n$. The inclusion of the compact exterior induces the same homology isomorphism by the retraction in [F2]. Thus $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n$.

The boundary of a small positive normal disk to $J_i$ maps to the $i$-th Alexander-duality coordinate generator: it meets $J_i$ once positively and misses every other component. Hence $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$ are the coordinate basis, with the positive orientation normalized as in [F3]. The $i$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$ is zero by its zero self-linking convention, and for $j\ne i$ its $j$-th coordinate is the defined linking number $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$. Therefore $[\delta_i]=[\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i]=\sum_jA_{ij}[\mu_j]$.

In Mayer–Vietoris for the filling, the map $H_1(\partial V_i)\to H_1(V_i)$ is onto and its kernel is generated by the meridian-disk boundary $\delta_i$. The map $H_0(\bigsqcup_i\partial V_i)\to H_0(X)\oplus H_0(\bigsqcup_iV_i)$ is injective: in coordinates it sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ to $(\sum_i a_i,-a_1,\ldots,-a_n)$. Exactness therefore gives $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$.

Since $A$ is invertible over $\mathbb Q$, for every $x\in\mathbb Z^n$ some positive integer $m$ clears the denominators of $A^{-1}x$, so $mx\in A\mathbb Z^n$ and each class is torsion. If $F,F'$ bound $mC,m'C$, pass to a common multiple $M$; the difference $(M/m)F-(M/m')F'$ is a 2-cycle $Z$. If $r[D]=0$, write $rD=\partial G$; the chain boundary identity gives $r(Z\mathbin{\cdot}D)=Z\mathbin{\cdot}\partial G=\partial Z\mathbin{\cdot}G=0$, hence $Z\mathbin{\cdot}D=0$. Thus the quotient is independent of the chosen bounding chain and multiple modulo integers. Replacing either cycle representative by a homologous one adds an integer by the same boundary identity.

Let $B$ be the slope-coordinate matrix $[\delta]=B[\mu]$ in $H_1(X;\mathbb Q)$; step 2.1 gives $B=A$. In the reverse filling, the slope-coordinate matrix is $B^{-1}$. Let $\widetilde J_i$ denote the core of the attached solid torus, oriented so the boundary longitude $\ell_i$ mapping to it satisfies $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\ell_i=1$. Since $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\mu_i=-1$, the image of $\mu_i$ in that solid torus is $-[\widetilde J_i]$. Define $H_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_Y(\widetilde J_i,\widetilde J_j)$ for $i\ne j$, and let $H_{ii}$ be the reverse-surgery framing determined by the slope $\mu_i$. For $i\ne j$, clear denominators in $[\mu_i]=\sum_k(B^{-1})_{ik}[\delta_k]$ and cap each $\delta_k$ by its meridian disk. The chain in $X$ realizing this homology relation misses every core; with $\delta_k\mathbin{\cdot}\ell_k=+1$, the capped disk in $V_k$ meets the oriented core $\widetilde J_j$ once positively if $k=j$ and not at all otherwise. Hence $(B^{-1})_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_Y(\mu_i,\widetilde J_j)=-H_{ij}$. The reverse diagonal framing is the reverse slope coefficient divided by $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\mu_i=-1$, so $H_{ii}=-(B^{-1})_{ii}$. Therefore $H=-B^{-1}=-A^{-1}$.

Each old meridian $\mu_i$ represents $-\widetilde J_i$ in its attached solid torus. Hence for distinct indices their linking equals the core-linking entry $H_{ij}$; for a self-pairing, a parallel meridian maps to the parallel core specified by the reverse framing, also giving $H_{ii}$. Thus $\lambda_Y([\mu_i],[\mu_j])=-(A^{-1})_{ij}$. The chain formula is additive in both cycles, by taking common multiples and summing bounding chains, so its matrix on the meridian basis gives $\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}$. If $x$ is replaced by $x+Az$, the value changes by $-z^Ty$; if $y$ is replaced by $y+Az$, it changes by $-x^Tz$, both integers because $A$ is symmetric and integral. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

If $A$ is a deformation retract of a topological space $X$, then for every
$n\geq 0$ and every abelian group $G$ the inclusion $i:A\hookrightarrow X$
induces an isomorphism
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(i_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups and identifies the positive meridian classes. The total-linking homomorphism in [F3] therefore corresponds to $\phi$; by [F4], $A_K$ is isomorphic to $N^{\mathrm{ab}}$ with the action induced by conjugation by a positive meridian, up to replacing that action by its inverse according to the left-versus-right lift convention.

Put $G_q=\ker(\phi\bmod q)$. For $g\in G_q$, write $\phi(g)=qk$ and set $n=g s^{-qk}\in N$. Then $g=n s^{qk}$, and the expression is unique because $\phi(s^{qk})=qk$. Thus $G_q$ is the split extension of $N$ by the infinite cyclic group generated by $s^q$, acting on $N$ by conjugation. By [F5] and [F1], $G_q$ is the fundamental group of $E_q$.

Abelianizing this split extension kills the commutators in $N$ and the relations $s^qns^{-q}=n$ for $n\in N$. By [F3], those relations impose $(t^q-1)A_K=0$ on $N^{\mathrm{ab}}$; if the inverse deck convention is used, $t^{-q}-1=-t^{-q}(t^q-1)$ generates the same submodule. The homomorphism $G_q\to\mathbb Z$, $g\mapsto\phi(g)/q$, splits by $1\mapsto s^q$, so $H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)\cong A_K/(t^q-1)A_K\oplus\mathbb Z[s^q]$.

The boundary of $E_q$ is a torus cover with basis the lift $\widetilde\mu$ of $\mu^q$ and a lifted longitude. Thicken $E_q$ and the filling solid torus by collars to form an open cover. By [F6], its Mayer–Vietoris map presents $H_1(\Sigma_q(K))$ as $H_1(E_q)$ modulo $[\widetilde\mu]$: the longitude lift maps to the core generator of the attached solid torus and eliminates that generator, while the filling meridian maps to zero there. The class $[\widetilde\mu]$ is $[s^q]$, the generator of the displayed free summand in step 3.1. Quotienting by it gives the stated isomorphism. [F1, F6, step 3.1, construct] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], cut $B^4$ along the thickening of the pushed-in disk-band surface, producing cut copies $B_1^4,\ldots,B_q^4$. First glue these copies only along the disk $0$-handle of the branch surface. A disk thickening is a $3$-ball in the boundary of each cut $4$-ball; joining the two face balls for consecutive copies is the standard boundary-connected-sum operation, so the resulting $4$-manifold is again a $4$-ball with one $0$-handle. For each surface band, the positive face of copy $k$ glued to the negative face of copy $k+1$ joins the two band-core arcs; its regular neighborhood is a $2$-handle $D^2\times D^2$ attached along $S^1\times D^2$. There are $q-1$ such seams and $2g$ bands, so the construction gives $2g(q-1)$ $2$-handles and no other handles.

For band $a_i$ and seam $k$, the attaching circle $C_{i,k}$ is obtained by joining its oriented core arc in the positive face of copy $k$ to the core arc in the negative face of copy $k+1$, with endpoints joined through the common disk $0$-handle. In the collar of $F$, closing either face arc through that disk gives the corresponding positive or negative push-off of the closed core cycle $a_i$. Simultaneously moving $a_i^-$ and $a_j$ through the product collar to $a_i$ and $a_j^+$ preserves linking, so symmetry of linking and [F3] give $\operatorname{lk}(a_i^-,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)=V_{ji}$. For two handles at the same seam, the positive-face and negative-face contributions are therefore $V_{ij}$ and $V_{ji}$, giving $V_{ij}+V_{ji}$; for the self-entry this is framing $2V_{ii}$. For handles at consecutive seams, only their common sheet contributes, and the reflection reverses one normal direction, giving $-\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)=-V_{ji}$ in the upper block; symmetry gives $-V_{ij}$ in the lower block. If the seams are separated by at least one unused seam, the attaching circles lie in disjoint sheet neighborhoods, so their linking is zero. These cases exhaust all pairs and give exactly $M_q(V)$.

In a normal disk to the branch surface, the $q$ cut sheets form the standard cyclic degree-$q$ branched disk; its map is $w\mapsto w^q$. Away from the branch locus, a positive meridian moves through the $q$ sheets cyclically, so the boundary exterior cover is the connected cover classified by the homomorphism $\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z/q$ sending $\mu$ to $1$. Its meridian boundary is the closed lift of $\mu^q$, which bounds the filling disk. By [F4] and uniqueness of the classified connected cover, the boundary with its branch marking is $\Sigma_q(K)$.
For $q=2$ there is one seam, so the block matrix has only its diagonal block $V+V^T$, as stated. [step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

Blockwise substitution in the definition shows $M_q(V')=P_q^TM_q(V)P_q$.
